On Sunday, October 19, the Laredo City Council voted to create a tax incentive plan aimed at parts of the city where the houses arrived years ago but the grocery stores never did. According to KGNS, the vote directs the city manager and the city's new economic development director to draft incentives for grocery stores, bookstores, medical clinics and other small businesses — with the focus on south Laredo, west Laredo and the Mines Road area.

The need is real and long-standing. Council members said south Laredo is growing quickly with new neighborhoods, but the daily essentials have not kept up. And in west Laredo and along Mines Road, families have waited decades for a grocery store. That word — decades — is doing a lot of work. Generations of residents in those areas have paid the same city taxes while driving across town for milk and a doctor's appointment.

The drafting job falls to Amber Holmes, the city's new economic development director. She will be formally introduced at the next council meeting, and according to KGNS the council expects an update within a month. That puts the first real look at the proposal somewhere around mid-November — after Election Day.

What we don't know yet

Webb Watch reads the fine print so you don't have to — and in this case, there is no fine print yet. The reporting published so far does not include a vote tally, a dollar figure, or a definition of what the "tax incentives" will actually be: property tax abatements, fee waivers, something else entirely. Staff told KGNS the plan is "not about handouts, but about removing barriers so small businesses can survive past their first five years." That framing is worth remembering when the draft appears — and worth checking against what the draft actually offers.

Here are the questions Webb Watch will be asking when the proposal surfaces:

  • Which council districts and neighborhoods are formally eligible — and who drew the map?
  • What exactly is the incentive, and what does it cost the city's tax base?
  • Will the draft be published for public comment before any vote to adopt it?
  • What keeps the incentives from flowing to the usual well-connected developers instead of the neighborhood grocers and clinics the vote was sold on?

Mayor Dr. Victor Treviño told KGNS the current process forces small businesses to pay high fees and navigate complex paperwork, and that bringing groceries and clinics closer to families could make a meaningful difference — especially for seniors, working parents and multigenerational families without reliable transportation. On the problem, the mayor is right: that is exactly what south and west Laredo families have been saying for years.

The timing is impossible to ignore. This vote landed two weeks before Election Day, with the mayor's office and city council seats on the November 3 ballot. A plan to bring grocery stores to neglected neighborhoods is good policy on any calendar — and it is also excellent campaign-season theater. The difference between the two will be written in the draft the council has not yet shown anyone. Webb Watch 956 will be there when it does.

Sources: KGNS, "Laredo council explores incentives for underserved areas," Oct. 20, 2026, by Kobe Arriaga; Laredo City Council meeting, Oct. 19, 2026.

— Walter Webb & Willa Webb, News Anchors, Webb Watch 956

title: Council Votes to Draft Tax Incentives for the Neighborhoods Growth Forgot
